Credentials end up everywhere: vaults, config files, chat, wikis, pipeline variables. The problem is rarely a missing tool. It is that nobody owns the whole picture. A platform fixes that with three things: a short service catalog, one named owner for every credential, and a lifecycle that runs the same way for all of them. The best credential is one that does not exist. Where a short-lived identity will do, use it before you vault a long-lived secret.

“Credential” covers a lot: passwords, API keys, SSH keys, tokens, database logins, cloud access keys and the secrets behind service accounts. In most companies each team grew its own way of handling them. One team uses a vault, another uses encrypted files, a third keeps them in pipeline variables, and some still sit in a shared document. Nothing is obviously broken until someone asks simple questions. Where does this credential live? Who owns it? When did it last change? Who has read it? If the answers take days to find, there is no control, only hope.
The fix is to treat credential management as a service with users, a menu and rules, and not as a collection of tools.

Start by writing down what the platform offers, who it is for, and what it does not cover. A short catalog is easier to adopt than a long one, and it gives each request a clear place to go. Service — For — What it does Privileged access for people — Admins, database owners, engineers on call — Approved, recorded sessions to servers, databases and cloud accounts, with no standing admin rights Secrets for applications — Developers and platform teams — Applications fetch secrets at runtime from one store. Nothing is copied into code or config.

Short-lived and dynamic credentials — Applications and pipelines — Credentials generated on demand that expire by themselves, so a leak has a short life Service account management — System owners — Every machine account has an owner, a rotation policy and a record of where it is used Inventory and reporting — Security, risk and audit — One view of what exists, who owns it, its age and its access history Decide the boundaries early. Certificates, for example, often have their own lifecycle and owners. If they are out of scope for the first release, say so in the catalog.

Four kinds of requester ask the platform for access. The platform is the only place that stores secrets, applies policy, rotates them and writes the log. Around it sit the systems a company already runs: a directory for sign-in and MFA, a service desk for approvals, and a SIEM for detection. The dots show a secret request traveling from a requester, through policy and the vault, to the system it protects. The named products are examples of each role, not an endorsement; any equivalent directory, service desk or SIEM fits the same slot.

Whatever the credential type, it should move through the same six stages. The ring shows the loop, and the owner and policy set at the start stay attached the whole way. The same loop applies to a database password, an API key or a service account. Retire is part of the loop: a credential nobody uses should not outlive the system it served.

h: Onboarding an application secret, start to finish
x: Ask, and name an owner The application team submits a request with the system, the environment, who owns the credential, and what it is used for. A credential without an owner is not issued. Guardrail No owner, no credential Evidence Intake record

Check whether the secret is needed at all If the workload runs on a cloud platform, it can often use a role that hands out temporary credentials. AWS, for instance, advises that workloads use temporary credentials from IAM roles, with no need to distribute long-lived keys. Only what cannot avoid a secret goes into the vault. Guardrail Short-lived identity first, stored secret second Evidence Design note

h: Check whether the secret is needed at all
x: Store it and set the policy The secret is created in the platform with a classification, a rotation policy, and a list of who and what may read it. Access is granted to the application, not to a shared human account. Guardrail Least privilege on read access Evidence Policy as configured

h: Store it and set the policy
x: Fetch at runtime The application asks the platform for the secret when it needs it. It is never pasted into code, config files or a pipeline variable that everyone can read. Guardrail Secret scanning blocks a commit that contains a credential Evidence Read log per request

Rotate without drama The platform changes the secret on schedule and the application picks up the new value. Rotation that needs a person and a change window rarely happens, so the design target is rotation nobody notices. Guardrail Automated rotation, with a failure alert Evidence Rotation history

Retire it When the application is decommissioned or the owner changes, the credential is revoked and removed. The owner confirms, and a missing confirmation escalates. Guardrail Regular owner attestation Evidence Revocation record

The password sits in a config file in a code repository. About fifteen people have seen it over the years. It has not changed since launch, because nobody is sure what would break. Nobody can say who actually owns it.

The application fetches a short-lived database login when it starts. No person ever sees or types it. It expires and is reissued automatically. The catalog names the owning team, and every read is logged.

Discovery is uncomfortable. The first inventory usually shows more secrets and fewer owners than anyone expected. Agree beforehand that this is a starting point, not a verdict on the teams. One platform for everything is a big target. It holds the keys to many systems, so it needs high availability, tight access of its own, and a tested plan for when it is down. Teams bypass it if it is slow. If onboarding takes weeks, credentials will reappear in pipelines and chat. Keep the front door quick. Legacy systems resist. Some cannot fetch a secret at runtime or accept a rotated value.

Track them as named exceptions with a plan. Migration costs real effort. Moving an application to runtime fetching is engineering work. Plan capacity with the teams, and do the highest-risk credentials first.

A tier describes blast radius. A credential belongs in the highest tier of anything it can change or mint access to, wherever it happens to be stored. Each tier gets a fixed set of controls: storage, rotation, access path, monitoring, approval and session recording. They get stronger towards Tier 0, and a credential that is valid in one tier is never valid in another. PAM products are sold as capabilities such as vaulting, session management and just-in-time access, not as tiers. Work out what each tier needs first, then see which tools supply it.

Most organizations have a vault. Far fewer can say which of their credentials are worth the most to an attacker, and which controls those credentials get. So the same standard ends up applied to a helpdesk password and to the account that administers the identity provider. Either the strong controls are too expensive to use everywhere, or the weak ones sit in front of things that matter. The usual attack path is short. Someone phishes a laptop, finds a credential that also works somewhere more valuable, and keeps moving. Nothing in that story needs a clever exploit.

It needs one credential that is valid in more places than it should be. Tiering is the habit of asking, for every credential, how far it could go if it were stolen, and then drawing a hard line at each step so that it cannot go further. Friction has a cost too. If every credential needs two approvers and a hardware key, people route around the process. If none do, the account that can rewrite your identity system is protected like a shared mailbox. Tiers are how you spend the friction where it buys the most.

h: Where the tier idea comes from
x: The Tier 0, 1, 2 language comes from Microsoft's Active Directory tier model, which was designed to contain unauthorized escalation of privilege in an on-premises Windows Server Active Directory environment. Microsoft's current guidance, the enterprise access model, builds on that model and widens it to cover on-premises, multiple clouds, internal and external users, and more. It did not throw the idea away. It renamed and split the tiers so they still make sense outside a single directory. In Microsoft's mapping, Tier 0 becomes the control plane: identity systems, centralized access enforcement and, where it is the only option, network controls.

h: Where the tier idea comes from
x: Tier 1 is split into a management plane for enterprise-wide IT management and a data and workload plane for per-workload management. Tier 2 becomes access pathways for users and for applications and APIs. Microsoft's wording differs a little between pages, so I read the mapping as a direction. One sentence from the architecture page is the reason Tier 0 gets the most attention: compromise of the control plane often enables indirect control of all other planes. Microsoft's privileged access strategy also defines three security levels: enterprise, specialized and privileged.

h: Where the tier idea comes from
x: At the privileged level, a person does not do sensitive work and everyday productivity tasks on the same account or device. I use that as the access-path rule for Tier 0. Two things here are my own. I use four tiers, with Tier 3 as a home for low-impact credentials. And I place individual credentials into tiers, where Microsoft's pages talk about planes and access pathways. The credential-level placement and the control set are my working method.

Read the diagram one row at a time. A request starts at the left, passes the controls on its tier's path, and only then reaches what it can change on the right. Tier 0 has four gates, Tier 1 three, Tier 2 two and Tier 3 one. Every row writes to the same audit log, kept outside the platform being audited. Each moving dot is a credential in use. It only reaches the right-hand side after passing every control on its own row. No arrow runs from one row to another, so a Tier 2 credential has no path into Tier 0.

The gates show the shape of the control set, not a product. Tier 0 holds the identity control plane: domain controllers, certificate authorities, the PAM vaults, and the admin plane of whatever runs your single sign-on. A cloud identity provider's global admin role is Tier 0 even with no server rack behind it. Tier 1 is the application, cloud and CI/CD estate. Tier 2 is workstation and helpdesk administration, the most common way in. Tier 3 is everyone else, the largest attack surface by count.

h: Six kinds of credential, and where each tends to land
x: A human admin password, a database login and an AI agent's token all open doors, but they are issued, stored and retired in different ways. I sort credentials into six classes by use, then place each one in a tier by what it can reach. Class — What it is — Where it usually lands — What decides the tier Human privileged — Admin accounts used by people: directory, cloud, database, helpdesk — Tier 0, 1 or 2 — What the account can administer. One person may hold three in three tiers.

h: Six kinds of credential, and where each tends to land
x: Service account — A non-interactive account that software uses to run on a host or in a directory — Tier of the systems it can reach — Its rights, and whether it allows interactive login. Directory rights mean Tier 0. Application secret — Database passwords, API keys and tokens an application uses at runtime — Mostly Tier 1, small ones in Tier 3 — What the secret unlocks: the data, the system, or another secret. Machine and NHI — Workload identities, pipeline identities, AI agent and MCP server credentials — Tier 1 at least when it can change infrastructure — The highest permission it holds.

h: Six kinds of credential, and where each tends to land
x: If it can create roles or edit a pipeline, it ranks above the system it was built for. Cloud key — Long-lived access keys, service principals and role assumptions in a cloud account — Tier 1, or Tier 0 when it can manage identity or permissions — Whether it only uses resources or can also change who may use them. Break glass — Emergency accounts for when the normal path is down — Tier 0, always — It can reach the control plane, so it carries the strongest controls. Machine and NHI credentials are the class I find least inventoried.

h: Six kinds of credential, and where each tends to land
x: An MCP server is a new case of the old service account problem: it usually holds a standing credential to whatever it connects to, and any agent that can reach it can use it. I treat it like a service account, with an owner, a tier, a scope and an expiry. The non-human identity at scale and agentic AI identity governance studies go further on this.

h: The control set for each tier
x: Every tier answers the same six questions: where the secret is stored, how it changes, what path leads to it, what watches its use, who approves a grant, and whether the session is recorded. The answers get stricter as the tier number falls. I kept the cells qualitative because intervals depend on your risk appetite and tooling. Control — Tier 0 — Tier 1 — Tier 2 — Tier 3 Storage — Vault or HSM-backed store, no other copy. Vault admins are separate from secret users. — Vault or secrets manager, fetched at runtime.

h: The control set for each tier

h: The workflow: classify, place, control, review
x: This is the loop I run for every credential, whether it already exists or someone is asking for a new one. Name an owner and find the credential Every credential needs a named person or team first. For existing credentials this is a discovery job across vaults, pipelines, directories, cloud accounts and code. For new ones it is an intake request saying what it is for and who answers for it. Guardrail No owner, no credential Evidence Inventory entry with owner and purpose

h: Name an owner and find the credential
x: Classify it Pick the class from the six above, then write down what it can do. Can it create or change other credentials? Edit a pipeline or a role? Log in interactively? What it can change decides the class. Where it is stored does not count. Guardrail Classification is based on permissions held, checked by someone other than the owner Evidence Classification record with the answers to those questions

Place it in a tier Apply the mint test: what is the highest tier this credential could reach, directly or by creating something else? That is its tier. Guardrail The owner cannot lower a tier alone. Tier 0 and Tier 1 placement needs security architecture sign-off Evidence Tier assignment with approver and date

Apply the tier's controls and close the old path Configure all six controls before the credential is issued or moved. Then close the old way in: a direct login, a copy in a config file or a shared account. Guardrail No issue until all six controls are set, and a test shows the old path is closed Evidence Policy as configured, plus the result of a deliberate attempt to use the old path

h: Apply the tier's controls and close the old path
x: Review, and move it when things change Review on a rhythm, using usage evidence instead of memory. Also review when something changes: new permissions, a new owner, a migration finishing. Move the credential if the answer to the mint test has changed. Guardrail Review decisions are driven by usage, and a permission change triggers a tier check Evidence Attestation record and usage report

This is an illustration, not a specific event. A pipeline holds a cloud key to deploy an application. First placement looks easy: a cloud key used by CI/CD, so Tier 1. Then the mint test. The role behind the key can create roles and attach policies in the cloud account, so the key can give itself anything, including admin rights over the account's identity layer. Its real tier is Tier 0 until the permissions change.

The key is long-lived and sits in a pipeline variable that every maintainer can read. The role was made broad so deployments would stop failing. Nobody can say which tier it belongs to. It is never reviewed because the pipeline works.

The pipeline gets short-lived credentials through a workload identity and no stored key remains. The role is cut down to deploy actions. Role creation is removed, so the credential drops to Tier 1. The owner, tier and expiry sit in the inventory. A change to the role triggers a tier check.

h: Where the PAM market fits the tiers
x: Tiers describe credentials. PAM products are packaged as capabilities, and the two do not line up one to one. Gartner defines PAM as a set of tools to control access and secure accounts that provide an elevated level of technical access, for human and machine accounts. Its capability list includes vaulting and rotation, session management, just-in-time privilege and provisioning, secrets management, command control, account discovery and onboarding, and privilege elevation. Those are the building blocks, and each tier needs a different mix.

h: Where the PAM market fits the tiers
x: Tier — What its controls need — Tool category that supplies it — Examples named elsewhere on this site Tier 0 — Vaulting, session recording, more than one approver, phishing-resistant sign-in, a break-glass path — PAM vault with session recording, plus hardware-key sign-in — CyberArk, Delinea, BeyondTrust; FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business Tier 1 — Dynamic secrets, visibility of combined cloud permissions, secret scanning before merge — Secrets management, cloud entitlement management, scanning — HashiCorp Vault, Infisical, GitGuardian; Wiz, Clutch Security, Sonrai Tier 2 — Unique local admin credentials, just-in-time elevation — Endpoint privilege management — BeyondTrust EPM, Delinea, ManageEngine PAM360 Across tiers — An inventory of non-human identities and usage-backed access reviews — NHI governance, identity governance and administration — SailPoint, Saviynt These are examples of each category, not a ranking.

h: Where the PAM market fits the tiers
x: No product here is the answer for every tier, and one suite may cover Tier 0 and Tier 2 well and still need another tool for pipelines.

The shape of the organization changes which categories to look at first. This is a profile view, not a league table. Large regulated enterprise. Audit depth matters most. Enterprise PAM suites such as CyberArk and BeyondTrust are the usual starting point. Mid-market. Standard compliance needs without heavy overhead. Mid-tier PAM such as Delinea Secret Server is the usual fit. Cloud-native and DevOps-first. Removing standing credentials and fast onboarding matter most. Cloud-native access platforms such as StrongDM and Teleport, plus cloud entitlement tooling such as Wiz, sit here. Compliance reporting is described as less mature, so pair them with identity governance if you need audit depth.

Small organization, first PAM deployment. The risk is having no tiering at all. Accessible platforms such as ManageEngine PAM360 get something in place quickly. Comparison sites describe enterprise suites as heavier on cost and deployment effort. I have not checked that against vendor pricing, so read it as direction only.

GitGuardian's 2026 report counts 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025. That figure covers public repositories only. I use it to show why a scanner that blocks a merge belongs in the Tier 1 controls. The second signal is consolidation. A 2026 tracker of non-human identity deals lists eight acquisitions or agreements between May and September 2026, with buyers from identity, network security, data security and credential management. It reads this as NHI turning from a standalone purchase into a capability inside larger platforms.

That tracker is a secondary source built from press releases and trade reporting, so treat the count as indicative. Check whether a platform you already own offers the NHI inventory before buying another tool. The credential platform strategy study is the next step if you want to see how these capabilities become one service with owners and a catalog.

Platform product owner — The tier standard, the control sets, the exception policy and the roadmap Security architecture — Tier definitions, sign-off on Tier 0 and Tier 1 placement, and boundary tests Credential owners — The classification of their credentials, the access list, the review attestation and the retirement Platform engineering — Running the gate and the vault, availability, and the break-glass path Security operations — Watching and responding to alerts on each tier Internal audit — Independent checking, separate from the people who run the controls One person never moves a credential down a tier alone.

The owner proposes, someone else approves, and the record shows both. Review the standard too. If every team asks for an exception to the same control, the control is wrong or the front door is too slow. Exceptions have owners and end dates. Anything that cannot meet its tier's controls, such as a legacy application needing a static password, goes on a register with a plan and a date. Measure coverage and drift.

Useful measures are the share of known credentials classified, credentials with no owner, credentials above their tier, Tier 0 systems still reachable by a direct path, and the age of the oldest unrotated secret.

Tier 0 is drawn too small. Teams list the domain controllers and forget the cloud identity provider's admin roles, the pipelines that deploy to the identity layer, or the vault. The vault stops at Tier 0. Many estates have a vault at the top and little below it, yet Tier 1 and Tier 2 are where a first foothold usually lands. Classification is done once. A Tier 1 credential can pick up permissions and become Tier 0 unnoticed. Review on change, not only on a calendar. The gate is a single point of failure.

If the vault or approval system is down during an incident, the response cannot be to wait for it. That is what a tested break-glass path is for. See break-glass access . Tiers turn into org charts. Tier 0 is for credentials that can mint other credentials, not a list of senior people. A product gets mistaken for a tier. A tool bought for one tier gets assumed to cover the rest. Temporary credentials stay forever. Accounts made to bridge a migration get forgotten because they were never meant to last. AI agents get standing access.
An agent that reviews access or manages secrets needs its own tier, scope and expiry. See AI agent credential sharing .

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits from how I run this kind of work. They are not a report on any one project. I ask what a credential can mint before I ask where it lives. Location is easy to see and misleading. Reach decides the tier. I finish Tier 0 before I start the rest. A half-built gate in every tier gives false comfort. A complete gate on the control plane is a smaller area I can defend properly. I keep the number of tiers small. When a team asks for a fifth tier, I look for a missing control in one of the four.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: I test the boundary by trying to cross it. Reading a policy proves little. Taking a low-tier credential and attempting to use it in a higher tier shows what is real. I write the tier definitions on one page and get them approved by the people they bind. If only security has read them, they last until the first incident review. I judge tools after I have written what each tier needs. Then I try two or three candidates on a small slice. That settles more than a comparison table. I give every temporary credential an expiry the day it is created.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: Cleanup backlogs do not get done. I test break-glass before go-live. It is part of the Tier 0 design, so it gets built and tried before the gate goes live. Admin rights granted as standing role membership outlive the task that justified them. Audits then depend on people remembering to take access back. The fix is elevation with two limits: a short window and a narrow scope. Each request opens a window, and the window closes on its own. I size the window from what people really did with the role. An advisory step can propose scope and duration, but the requester and the approver still decide.

Administrative rights were granted as standing role membership. Someone needed access for a migration, got added to a role, and stayed in it long after the migration ended. Every audit relied on people remembering to revoke what they no longer needed, and remembering is a weak control. A privileged account that is always on is always worth stealing. MITRE ATT&CK lists Valid Accounts (T1078) as a technique that adversaries use for initial access, persistence, privilege escalation and defense evasion. A standing admin role hands them all four for as long as the account exists.
Shrinking the hours in which an account is privileged shrinks what a stolen credential can do.

h: Two terms that get mixed up
x: Just-in-time (JIT) is about time. Privilege is activated when a task needs it and ends when the window ends. JEA has a precise meaning at Microsoft: Just Enough Administration, a PowerShell feature. You write role capability files ( .psrc ) that list the cmdlets, functions and commands a role may run, and a session configuration ( .pssc ) that says who can connect, which roles they get and which identity the session runs as. Users connect to a constrained endpoint. The session can run as a virtual account, which Microsoft describes as a temporary local account that is destroyed when the session ends.

h: Two terms that get mixed up
x: In this case study the title says “Just-Enough-Access”, which is the wider idea: give the smallest scope that does the job, on any platform. I write “JEA” only when I mean Microsoft’s feature, and I write “just-enough scope” for the general idea. The two work well together. JIT limits when, and just-enough scope limits what.

The diagram compares one engineer over one week. Standing access is a constant bar. Elevation is a set of short windows, each one requested, approved, used and closed. Illustrative only. The top part shows the shape: a constant bar against short windows. The dots show one request traveling through its four steps. The windows in the diagram are not measured data.

h: The same idea in different places
x: Elevation looks different depending on what you are elevating into. These are the patterns I reach for, in the order I usually roll them out. Target — How the window is made — Watch for Cloud roles — The person is eligible for the role and activates it for a limited time. Microsoft Entra PIM does this for Entra roles and Azure resource roles, with approval, MFA and a justification if you require them. — The role is still as powerful as a permanent one. Microsoft says there is no difference in access between eligible and permanent, only in how often the person needs it.

h: The same idea in different places
x: Directory and application groups — Group membership is activated for a time. PIM for Groups offers this, and groups can control Entra roles, Azure roles and other application access. In on-premises Active Directory on Windows Server 2016 or later, a membership can carry an expiry time. — Microsoft recommends approval for eligible members of groups that elevate into Entra roles. Check what the group really unlocks. Servers — A session through a PAM broker, where the broker uses the credential and the person never sees it. Or a temporary account that exists only for the window.

h: The same idea in different places
x: For PowerShell-managed tasks, a JEA endpoint limits the commands. — Microsoft warns that JEA does not protect against users who are already administrators, and that wildcards and commands such as Start-Process can let someone escape the role. Databases — In my approach, a brokered session with a login or role that is granted for the window and revoked when it ends. — Applications often hold their own database logins. Those belong to the credential platform, not to this flow.

h: The same idea in different places
x: Kubernetes — In my approach, short-lived access bound to a narrow role, with cluster-wide admin reserved for a small, approved set of cases. — Cluster roles can be broader than anyone intended. Review what each role really allows before you size a window for it. A vendor-neutral summary comes from the UK National Cyber Security Center. Instead of using a credential to reach an administration interface, the administrator uses it to request access, and if the request is approved a temporary credential is issued.

h: The same idea in different places
x: The NCSC also says that shortening how long an administration credential can be used cuts the attacker’s window if one is stolen.

Ask for a task, not a role The requester names the target, the task, the ticket or change number and how long they think they need. “Admin on everything for a week” is not a valid request. Microsoft’s PIM has a ticket field, but its documentation says it is information only and does not check the number against a ticketing system. So the service desk does the checking. Guardrail No open ticket, no request Evidence Request record

h: Ask for a task, not a role
x: Prove who they are, properly Sign-in goes through single sign-on, with multi-factor authentication and conditional access. The details matter here. PIM can require MFA on activation, and it can require a Conditional Access authentication context, for example a specific authentication strength or a compliant device. If someone has just reauthenticated for one activation, Microsoft says they are not asked again within ten minutes for other eligible roles. Guardrail No MFA, no activation Evidence Sign-in log

Get an advisory proposal A policy-aware assistant reads the request and proposes a scope and a duration, using what the role has really been used for. It is a suggestion. The requester can change it, and the approver sees it next to the request. The proposal can never go above the maximum the policy sets for that role. Guardrail Proposal capped by policy, humans decide Evidence Proposal and final choice, both recorded

Approve by policy, or by a person Roles with low risk and a pre-agreed use can be approved by policy. Anything touching production or the identity systems needs a named person. Approvals flow through the service desk (ServiceNow in my setup). PIM itself says approvers cannot approve their own activation requests, and that an unapproved request expires after 24 hours and has to be submitted again. I apply the same rule to every platform: the requester is never the approver. Guardrail Separation of duties Evidence Approver, time, reason

h: Approve by policy, or by a person
x: Open the window The eligible assignment is activated, or the group membership is added with an expiry, or the broker session starts. The window carries its own end time from the first second. PIM’s activation maximum can be set between 1 and 24 hours per role. Guardrail Smallest role that does the task, end time set at the start Evidence Activation record with start and end

Work, and leave a trail Everything the person does is logged, and on brokered sessions recorded. Logs go to the SIEM so that the people who hold the privilege cannot edit the record of using it. Guardrail Logs stored outside the elevation tool Evidence Session record or audit log tied to the ticket

Close it and look back When the timer ends or the task is marked complete, the access is removed by the system. A follow-up ticket is never needed. Afterwards I look at windows that closed with no privileged action in them, because they tell me the role or the window was too big. Guardrail Expiry enforced by the system, not by memory Evidence Expiry event and the review of unused windows

h: When the work runs past the window
x: Change windows overrun. I handle this as a fresh request with fresh approval, never as a silent extension. The requester says why more time is needed, and the approver can see how long the first window ran. Microsoft’s documented extend and renew features apply to role assignments that are about to expire. When a user asks for one, an administrator has to approve it. For an activation that is running out, the simple rule is to request again.

h: When the elevation path is down
x: The identity provider, the service desk or the broker can be unavailable at the worst moment. Break glass stays available for exactly this. Microsoft’s guidance for Entra is two or more cloud-only emergency accounts, made permanently active and not eligible, with phishing-resistant sign-in, alerts on every use, and a check at least every 90 days. The NCSC says to protect the break-glass process carefully. I cover the design in Break-Glass Emergency Access Design .

h: Accounts that cannot be elevated just in time
x: A scheduled task or a service account has no person to request anything at 3 a.m. Forcing it through this flow only produces a service account with permanent approval. These identities go to the credential platform instead, where they get an owner, a rotation policy or a short-lived credential. The two case studies fit together: Credential Management Platform Strategy for the machine side and Non-Human Identity at Scale for the scale problem.

h: Example: fixing a network rule in one subscription
x: This is an illustration, not a specific event. The times are made up to show the shape.

The engineer has held a broad role on the whole subscription since a project two years ago. The role was never reviewed, because removing it would mean a ticket nobody owns. A stolen session would work at any hour, on everything in the subscription.

The engineer is eligible for a narrower role on one resource group. They ask for 90 minutes, citing the change ticket. The assistant suggests 90 minutes and the network role, and the approver accepts. MFA and conditional access run at activation, and the window closes at the 90-minute mark. The activation, the approver and the reason are all in the log. For the wider picture of zero standing privilege, brokers and session recording, see PAM Modernization & Zero Standing Privilege . None of these standards prescribes just-in-time access by name. Time-bound elevation is one practical way to meet what they ask. AC-6(7) — Review assigned privileges periodically, and reassign or remove them where they no longer fit.

AC-6(9) , AC-6(10) — Log the execution of privileged functions, and prevent non-privileged users from executing them. AC-5 — Identify and document duties, and define access authorizations that support separation of duties. AU-2 , AU-12 — Deciding which events are logged, and generating the audit records for them. NIST SP 800-207 — Zero Trust tenet on sessions — Access to individual enterprise resources is granted on a per-session basis. CIS Controls v8 — 5.4 , 6.8 — Restrict administrator privileges to dedicated administrator accounts, and define role-based access control with reviews at least annually.

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — A.8.2 , A.8.3 — Privileged access rights are restricted and managed, and access to information is restricted under the access control policy. MITRE ATT&CK — T1078 — Not a control. It describes how adversaries use valid accounts. Its mitigations include multi-factor authentication and privileged account management.

Elevation product owner — The catalog of elevatable roles, default windows, the roadmap and what is in scope Identity engineering — Running the activation, approval and expiry mechanisms and their integrations Role owners — What each role is for, the tasks it covers, who may approve it and who may be eligible Approvers — The decision on each request, with enough context to say no Security operations — Watching elevations and break-glass use in the SIEM Internal audit — Independent checking, separate from those who run the controls Changes to windows and scopes go through change control.

A longer default window is a risk decision, and it has a named owner. The advisory step is governed like any other policy input. Its rules, caps and changes are documented and approved, and its proposals are logged beside the final decision. Exceptions have owners and end dates. Anything left as standing access sits on a register and is reviewed on a rhythm.

Approval fatigue. If approvers see hundreds of requests a week, they start approving without reading. Pre-agreed roles can go through policy, so people only look at the risky ones. Windows set wrong in both directions. Too short and people get cut off in the middle of a change. Too long and the window is standing access with a new name. Eligible becomes the new standing. If everyone is eligible for everything, the list of eligible people is the list of targets. Eligible accounts still need strong sign-in and regular review. The elevation path becomes a dependency.

When the identity provider or service desk is down, nobody can fix anything. This is why the fallback has to be built and tested first. JEA endpoints with loose roles. Microsoft warns against wildcards in role capabilities and against allowing commands such as Start-Process, and notes that a local administrator can change a JEA configuration. A JEA endpoint is only as tight as its role file. Legacy systems with no concept of expiry. Some platforms cannot remove access on a timer. A broker session or a scripted removal can close the gap, and the rest goes on the exceptions register. Adoption friction.
Engineers who used to have instant access now wait. If the wait is long or the form is long, they will look for ways around it.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits I keep, not a checklist from any one project. I map the role to its tasks before I pick a number. A default window copied from somewhere else is a guess. A window sized from what people really did with the role is something I can defend. I keep the form short. Target, task, ticket, length. Every extra field is a reason to look for a shortcut. I start where the platform already does the work. Cloud and directory roles first, because activation, approval and expiry exist there. Those early results buy trust for the harder platforms.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: I keep the advisory step advisory. It proposes, people decide, and I log both. I also look at where people disagree with it, because that is where the policy needs work. I test the fallback before I remove standing access. Not after. The day you take the last standing role away is the wrong day to learn that break glass does not work. I sit with approvers. An approver who cannot see the ticket, the target and the requested length cannot make a good decision, so the request has to carry that context. I publish time to access.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: Engineers accept a new control more easily when they can see that somebody is watching how long it takes. I keep service accounts out of this flow from day one. They have a different answer, and mixing the two slows both. The longer version of how I run this kind of work is in How I Run a Privileged Access Program .

A migration moves more than accounts. The old tool also carries controls, approvals, integrations and habits, and some of them were never written down. I start by analyzing what the current tool does, what it fails to do and what is inside it. Then I run discovery and get the plan signed off before anything moves. Waves follow dependency, risk, access criticality and rollback readiness. At cutover every secret is rotated, because whatever sat in the old vault has to be treated as known to the people who administered it.

A privileged access migration has to preserve controls, user journeys, integrations and operational continuity. Moving the accounts is the easy part. The hard part is everything around them: the approval that fires before a checkout, the nightly script that reads a password from the old tool’s API, the alert someone relies on, the administrator who knows which safe to open at 2 a.m. The old tool has usually been running for years. People built on it without telling anyone. If you only copy the inventory you will move the accounts and lose the behavior.

Most of my planning work is about finding that behavior early and deciding, on paper, what happens to each piece of it. I led the analysis of a legacy PAM tool and the capability mapping for the target-state decision. The method below is what that work taught me to do every time.

h: Start with the tool you already have
x: When an organization already has a tool and wants to move to a new one, I do not start with the new one. I start with three questions about the old one. What does it do today? Features, integrations, and how people really use it, which is often different from how it was designed. What is it failing to do? The gaps that made the organization want to move. These become requirements for the target, so they are worth writing down in the owners’ own words. What is inside it? The inventory of accounts, safes or folders, policies and owners.

h: Start with the tool you already have
x: I treat this as a claim to be checked, not as a fact. The answers feed a capability map: one row per thing the old tool does, and what the target does about it. That map is what the target-state decision and the later control-equivalence checks are built on.

I split the inventory into five classes, because each one migrates differently and each one has a different person to ask. Class — Examples — The question I ask — What makes it tricky Human privileged — Domain, local and root admin accounts, database administrators — Who actually uses it, and how often? — People have habits and saved sessions. Workflow and approval rules have to match or people work around them. Service and application — Service accounts, application and database logins, API keys — What reads this, and what breaks if it changes? — Changing the value can stop a job.

This is where hidden dependencies live. Shared — Accounts used by a team, vendor or help desk — Who is in the group, and who is it really? — Without individual accountability, the session record is the only evidence of who did what. Machine — SSH keys, certificates, tokens, secrets used by pipelines and workloads — Could this be short-lived instead of stored? — Some stores hold them in fields nobody tracks. Some cannot accept a rotated value.

Break glass — Emergency accounts for when sign-in or the platform is down — Does it work if everything else is broken? — It must follow organization policy and be tested, because it is the way back in during a failed cutover.

h: Discovery: finding what nobody wrote down
x: The exported inventory tells you what the tool believes. Discovery tells you what is true. I use several sources and compare them, because each one is wrong in a different way. Source — What it shows — How it misleads The old tool’s own account list — What was onboarded, with owners and policies — Owners have left, and accounts were added and never removed. Usage and audit logs of the old tool — Who checked out what, when it last happened, which API clients called it — Quiet accounts may still matter once a quarter or once a year.

h: Discovery: finding what nobody wrote down
x: Scans of servers, directory and network devices — Privileged accounts that exist but were never vaulted — A scan finds accounts, not the reason they exist. Scheduled tasks, scripts and pipeline code — Jobs that call the old tool or hard-code a credential — Code search misses what lives in someone’s head or on a laptop. Tickets and approval history — Real request patterns and who approves — People raise tickets differently from how the process says. Interviews with owners — Purpose, business impact and the workarounds — People forget, and some things were set up by someone who has moved on.

For every credential that something other than a person uses, I record who or what reads it, how (API call, agent, script, scheduled task or a hard-coded copy), how often, what stops working if the value changes, and who can fix it. That record decides the wave a credential goes into and whether it can be rotated at cutover. A hard-coded use is not a reason to skip the credential. It is a work item for its owner, with a date, before the wave.

Before anything moves, every row of the capability map gets one decision. The matrix below is illustrative. The capabilities are typical, and the decisions are examples of the kind of result I record, not findings from a real estate.

Old tool capability — Target tool capability — Gap — Decision Checkout needs approval and a valid ticket — Approval workflow with a ticketing integration — Approver lists need rebuilding in the new naming convention — Equivalent once groups are mapped Session recording for the highest tier — Brokered sessions with recording — Storage and retention differ — Accept, with retention set in the design Scheduled rotation of service accounts — Scheduled rotation with dependency handling — One class of accounts cannot be rotated automatically — Compensating process and a named exception with an end date Break-glass retrieval — Emergency access route — Must work if the identity provider is unavailable — Rebuild to organization policy and test before first production wave A custom report an auditor asks for — Built-in reporting — Different fields — Rebuild, then confirm with the auditor A feature nobody has used in years — None — Not needed — Retire, with the owner’s sign-off Every gap ends in one of a short list of decisions: equivalent, better, a compensating control, an accepted gap with an owner and end date, or retired on purpose.

The plan has two halves. First, plan and prove: understand the old tool, discover, decide and sign off, then build a small proof in Dev. Then move and retire: rehearse in pre-production, go live in waves, rotate, and switch the old tool off. Rollback stays open across the second half. The dot follows one batch of accounts from the old tool to its retirement. The words on the arrows are what has to exist before the next stage starts.

Analyze the current tool What it does, what it fails to do, what it holds. Findings are written in a short document that the owners read and correct. Guardrail No design before the current state is written down Evidence Current-state analysis and capability map

Run discovery and reconcile the inventory Compare the tool’s list with scans, logs, code and interviews. Every difference is either fixed or logged. Then each owner confirms their part of the list. Guardrail Inventory signed off by owners before waves are planned Evidence Reconciliation report and owner sign-offs

h: Run discovery and reconcile the inventory
x: Map dependencies For each non-human credential: who reads it, how, how often and what breaks. Hard-coded uses become tasks for their owners. Guardrail No credential is rotated without a known list of readers Evidence Dependency register

Decide control equivalence and sign off the plan Every capability row gets a decision. The migration plan, the processes around it and the wave plan go to the stakeholders for sign-off. Guardrail No blank decisions at the checkpoint Evidence Signed control-equivalence matrix and migration plan

h: Decide control equivalence and sign off the plan
x: Write and approve the foundations The password policy is reviewed and refined. Naming conventions for groups and roles are refined, approved and documented. Vaulting security is documented and approved by the business. Break glass is onboarded following organization policy. Integrations with ServiceNow, Entra for SSO and MFA, and the SIEM are documented. Guardrail Nothing is built before its policy is approved Evidence Approved policy, naming, vaulting and integration documents

Prove it in Dev A small, limited proof with a few accounts from each class. The point is to find the surprises while they are cheap. Guardrail Written go/no-go criteria to leave Dev Evidence Proof results and sign-off

Rehearse in pre-production and run in parallel Full-shape rehearsal, with integrations, failover and break glass exercised. The old tool keeps running for the accounts not yet moved. Guardrail Break glass tested and high availability and disaster recovery exercised before go-live Evidence Test results, drill record

h: Rehearse in pre-production and run in parallel
x: Cut over in waves, then rotate Each wave has its own rollback criteria and an owner who accepts it. After acceptance, every secret in the wave is rotated and the old copy is retired. Guardrail Rotation before the old vault is retired Evidence Wave acceptance record, rotation history

h: Cut over in waves, then rotate
x: Decommission and keep the evidence Remove the old tool’s own privileged access to targets, archive its logs and session recordings, and switch it off on an agreed date. Guardrail No switch-off until archive is readable and owned Evidence Decommission record, archive index
A database service account is owned by the infrastructure team. Nobody has checked it out in a long time. It looks safe to move early and rotate on day one.

h: What discovery shows and what I do
x: A scheduled job reads it through the old tool’s API every night. I record the job and its owner, and ask the owner to repoint it to the target before the wave. The account moves in the same wave as the job, and is rotated after the job has run once successfully.

A wave is a set of accounts that move together, with a date, an owner and a way back. I order them using four criteria. Criterion — The question — Effect on order Dependency — What reads this, and does it move in the same wave? — Things that depend on each other go together. Risk — What is the exposure today, and what could a bad move cause? — High exposure argues for early, but only once the route is proven.

Access criticality — How badly does the business suffer if this access fails? — The most critical access goes after a rehearsal, with an owner present. Rollback readiness — Can we go back, and have we tried? — No wave without a tested way back. In practice the first wave is small and low in criticality, so the team learns on something forgiving. Break glass is ready before the first production wave, because it is the way back in if something goes wrong.

Parallel running. Both tools are live for a while. The rule I keep is that one tool is the source of truth for any given account at any given time, and everybody knows which. Two tools each changing the same password is a recipe for lockouts. Cutover. For each wave the accounts are verified in the target, the owners repoint their consumers, the old tool’s entries for those accounts go read-only, and the owner accepts the wave. Rollback criteria. I write them before the wave, in plain language, with the decision maker named.

Typical triggers: A critical dependency cannot read its credential and cannot be fixed inside the agreed window. Sessions cannot be brokered for a critical group of systems. The approval or ticket integration fails, so access cannot be granted in a controlled way. The break-glass test fails. Rollback is simple until secrets are rotated, because the old vault still holds values that work. After rotation the old values are dead, so a rollback means restoring or re-setting them.
For that reason I agree the point where the rollback window closes with the owners, and I put it right after acceptance and the first successful run of the dependent jobs.

The old vault’s secrets should be treated as exposed to the old administrators. They could read them, the old backups hold them, and export files from the migration may have copies. Nobody needs to have done anything wrong for that to be true. It is a question of who could have seen them. So each secret is changed after it lands in the target, and then the export files and old copies are removed and recorded as removed. For people’s memorised passwords, NIST SP 800-63B advises against forced periodic changes without evidence of compromise.
Vaulted privileged credentials are different: the tool sets them, nobody types them, and a change costs almost nothing.

Everything now sits on cloud, and the platform will hold the keys to a lot. Before a production wave I want to know the target can lose a component without losing the service, that a second region exists with agreed recovery objectives, that a restore has actually been tried, and that break glass works when the platform or the identity provider does not. NIST SP 800-53 CP-10 expresses the same thing: recover the system to a known state within a time consistent with the recovery objectives.

The old tool is not finished when the last wave moves. Its audit logs and session recordings often have to be kept for a retention period, so I plan who can read them, in what format, where they live and for how long. Remove the old tool’s reach. It had accounts on targets to rotate and log in. Those accounts, and the integrations that used them, are removed. Archive the evidence. Logs and recordings go to an archive with an owner, a read process and a retention date taken from the organization’s own requirements.

NIST SP 800-53 AU-11 asks for records to be retained for an organization-defined period. Where PCI DSS applies, requirement 10.5.1 asks for at least 12 months of audit log history, with the most recent three months immediately available. Check the archive can be read. Someone opens a sample before the old tool is switched off. Switch off on an agreed date. Licenses, backups, keys and exported files are handled and recorded.

1. Analyze and discover Current-state analysis, capability map, discovery, dependency register, inventory sign-off. Done when Every owner has signed their part of the inventory, and every capability has a decision. 2. Dev, a small proof A limited proof with accounts from each class, and the foundation documents drafted. Done when The written go/no-go criteria are met and the surprises are in the plan. 3. Pre-production Rehearsal with integrations, parallel running, failover and break glass exercised. Done when Test results are accepted and the wave plan has dates and owners. 4. Production go-live in waves Cutover, acceptance and rotation for each wave, with rollback criteria.

Done when Every in-scope account is accepted in the target, or sits on the exception register. 5. Handover and retire Runbook per environment, troubleshooting and operations documents approved, the old tool archived and switched off. Done when The customer operates the platform from the documents and the decommission record is signed.

Dependencies that nobody listed. A script, a report or a scheduled task uses a credential and only shows itself when the value changes. Copying the mess. h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits I keep. They are not a record of any single project. I read the old tool as a source of requirements. Machine identities get created faster than anyone records them. The first job is one inventory, with a named owner against every entry and a flag on every entry that has none. A simple score turns that inventory into a queue. I rank on three things: how long since the secret changed, how much it can do, and whether anyone owns it. Evidence of exposure and last use come next. The best fix removes the secret. Where a workload can use a role, federation or a short-lived token, do that before you rotate a static key.

A non-human identity is anything that signs in without a person at the keyboard: a service account, an API key, a token, a certificate, a workload identity, an OAuth app, a bot, and more and more often an AI agent. Each one is a way into a system, and each one raises the same questions as a person’s account. Who is it for? What can it reach? When was it last changed? Who would notice if it were misused? The difference is how they come into being. A developer creates a service account to unblock a release.

A pipeline needs a token, so someone makes one. A vendor integration asks for an OAuth grant, and an admin clicks yes. None of these goes through the process a new employee goes through, and none of them has a manager who changes jobs and hands the account over. So ownership gets lost at handoff, credentials outlive the systems that issued them, and audits fall back on belief. “We think the team rotates these” is a sentence I have heard in more than one review, and it is not evidence.

OWASP’s Non-Human Identities Top 10 puts improper offboarding first, which it describes as inadequate deactivation or removal of non-human identities when they are no longer needed. That is the same failure in different words. I have left out any ratio of machines to people. Figures like that circulate widely, and I could not trace one to a primary source with a method I trust. The program does not depend on the number. It depends on knowing your own inventory.

Kind — Where it tends to live — What usually goes wrong Service accounts — Directories, databases, operating systems, cloud IAM — Created for one project, kept for ten. The password is shared and never changes. API keys and access keys — Cloud accounts, SaaS admin consoles, config files — Copied into code or chat. No expiry, broad scope. Tokens — Pipeline variables, developer machines, repositories — Tied to the person who made it, so it breaks or lingers when they move on. Certificates and keys — Load balancers, services, key stores — Expiry surprises, and private keys copied between environments.

Workload identities — Cloud roles, managed identities, cluster service accounts — Roles that started narrow and grew permission by permission. OAuth apps and integrations — SaaS platforms, identity provider consent screens — Third-party access granted once and never reviewed. Bots and automation — Chat tools, ticketing, scheduled jobs — Run with an admin login because that was quickest. AI agents — Agent platforms, tool servers, developer tooling — Share one key across agents, or act on a person’s delegated token. See One Key, Every Agent . How the credentials themselves are stored, issued and rotated is covered in Credential Management Platform Strategy .
This page picks up one step earlier: finding what exists, deciding who answers for it, and deciding what to fix first.

Five kinds of source tell you what exists. Cloud IAM lists roles, access keys and app registrations. CI/CD systems list pipeline variables and tokens. Code scanning finds secrets sitting in repositories and their history. Vaults know what is stored, when it last rotated and when it was last read. Directories hold the service accounts. Each source sees a different slice, and the same identity often appears in two or three of them under different names. Everything flows into one inventory. From there each record needs an owner, then a score, and then it lands in a queue where someone fixes it.

A re-scan afterwards confirms the fix, and an evidence log keeps who, what and when for every step. The scanning is read-only. Fixing happens in the source system, by the owner. Each dot is one identity: found in a source, merged into the inventory, given an owner, scored and queued. The numbers on the boxes match the first five steps of the workflow below. The dashed lines into the evidence log show that every stage writes to it.

Seven steps. Each has a guardrail, which is the rule that keeps the step honest, and the evidence an auditor can ask to see. Discover from every source you can reach Start with the two or three sources that hold the most: usually cloud IAM, the main vault and the code repositories. Keep a register of sources, with a person who answers for each one, so a gap in coverage is visible and not silent. Guardrail Read-only discovery access, every source has an owner Evidence Source register with last successful scan date

h: Discover from every source you can reach
x: Merge into one inventory Give each identity one record with a few required fields: type, system, environment, created date, last rotated, last used, privilege level, owner and the source that found it. When two sources describe the same identity, merge them. When a record is missing a field, flag it and keep it. A half-filled record is still better than no record. Guardrail Required fields, and incomplete records are flagged, not dropped Evidence Inventory export with field completeness

Assign a named owner An owner is a person or a team that will answer for the identity, change it and retire it. Where nobody claims it, the record goes to the owner of the system it touches, and from there to a review queue with a deadline. Ownership has to be accepted, because being named by someone else does not make a person accountable. Guardrail No owner within the agreed time raises the score and routes to review Evidence Owner acceptance record

Score every identity the same way Use one formula, version it, and store the inputs next to the result so anyone can see why an identity ranks where it does. The factors and a worked example are in the next section. The score orders the work. It says nothing about the quality of a team. Guardrail One versioned formula, inputs kept with the score Evidence Score history per identity

h: Score every identity the same way
x: Fix at the source, in a fixed order Work down the queue. For each identity ask four questions in order. Is it still used? If not, retire it. Can the workload use a role, federation or a short-lived token? If so, replace the secret. Is the access wider than the job needs? Cut it. Is a static secret still unavoidable? Rotate it, and set the next rotation. Retiring comes before rotating, because rotating something nobody uses only adds work. Guardrail Retire first, remove the secret second, rotate last Evidence Change record in the system that owns the identity

h: Fix at the source, in a fixed order
x: Verify, then close A fix is closed when a re-scan shows the change and the owner confirms it. If the owner stays silent, the item escalates. Closing a ticket on someone’s word is how stale findings come back at the next audit. Guardrail Closure needs a re-scan result, and a ticket status alone is not enough Evidence Before and after scan, owner confirmation

Most PAM programs stop once the passwords are in a vault. The risk that is left is access that never expires. Modernizing means four things working together: vault the secret, rotate it, put a recorded session in front of it, and grant access only for the length of the task. Every one of those steps has to leave evidence an auditor can check without asking you to explain it.

Privileged accounts are the ones that can change the system itself: domain admins, database owners, root on servers, cloud administrators, and service accounts with wide rights. Attackers want them because a valid account looks like normal activity. MITRE ATT&CK tracks this as Valid Accounts (T1078) . Standing privilege makes it worse. If an admin group has forty members, then forty people, and any malware running as them, can reach every system that group covers, at any hour, whether or not they are doing admin work. When an admin signs in interactively to a workstation, credential material can stay in that machine’s memory.
That is why credential dumping (T1003) is such a common step right after the first foothold.

The vault is there, but the old door is still open. Passwords are stored centrally, yet admins can still log in directly because nobody closed the direct path. Rotation skips the hard accounts. The accounts nobody dares touch are the ones hard-coded in scripts or shared between teams. Session recording is patchy. Some systems are covered and some are not, so a reviewer cannot answer “what did they actually do?” “Temporary” access is never taken back. Nobody owns the expiry.

A privileged session has to pass through a few controls, in order. If one is missing, the others can be walked around. The diagram shows the path a request takes, and where evidence is written along the way. A request passes five checkpoints in order. The audit store sits outside the systems being administered, so the people being recorded cannot change the record. Step 6 removes the access again. Products split this work differently, but the functions are the same.

In CyberArk’s self-hosted architecture, for example, the Vault stores the secrets, the Central Policy Manager (CPM) generates new passwords and replaces them on the target machines, and the Privileged Session Manager (PSM) records sessions and can restrict commands. Other platforms combine or separate these roles. What matters is that all of the functions exist and that none can be skipped. CyberArk architecture reference .

One shared database admin password, known to a whole team. Not changed for over a year, because changing it might break a script. The engineer logs in directly. Nothing records what they ran. After an incident, nobody can say who did what.

The engineer asks for two hours on that database, citing the incident ticket. The on-call manager approves from their phone. The session runs through the broker and is recorded. At the end, access closes and the credential is rotated. The recording is linked to the ticket.

Zero Standing Privilege means nobody holds admin rights by default. Access is created for a task and removed when it ends. This lines up with a tenet in NIST’s Zero Trust Architecture (SP 800-207): access to each resource is granted per session, with the least privilege needed to finish the task. Illustrative only. The point is the shape: with standing access the attack surface is the whole week. With just-in-time access it is only the short windows when someone had an approved reason to be there.

Move people to phishing-resistant sign-in in risk order: privileged users first, then people who reach high-risk apps, then everyone else. One company-wide date puts the heaviest support load on the day you can least afford it. Recovery decides whether the program works. If a lost key can be fixed with a text message or a password reset, an attacker will use that route instead of the strong one. Keep a fallback during each wave and retire it only when adoption and help-desk data say the wave is stable. Legacy apps and break-glass accounts get named plans, not quiet exceptions.

Most workforces still sign in with a password and something extra: a text message code, an app code, or a push notification to approve. That is better than a password alone, and it is still phishable. A convincing fake sign-in page can collect the password and the code together and replay them to the real site. CISA’s phishing-resistant MFA fact sheet lists SMS and voice codes, push notifications without number matching and app one-time codes without number matching as forms of MFA that remain open to phishing, and it calls SMS and voice a last resort. Phishing-resistant sign-in closes that gap.

It also creates a project that is easy to get wrong. A blanket rollout can lock out the users least ready for it, while the accounts most worth protecting wait on the same generic timeline as everyone else. The administrator who can change every other account’s access ends up in the same queue as a part-time user of a low-risk tool. So I start with practical questions. Who needs it most? What happens the day someone loses the device? Which applications cannot take a modern sign-in at all?
And how will we know that people use the new method and do not drift back to the old one?

WebAuthn. The W3C Web Authentication standard. It defines an API for creating and using public key credentials that are scoped to the site that created them. A credential can only be used with the same relying party it was registered with, which is why a look-alike site gets nothing useful. Passkey. The FIDO Alliance describes a passkey as a FIDO authentication credential that lets a person sign in with the same process they use to unlock their device: a biometric, a PIN or a pattern. Device-bound and synced.

FIDO describes synced passkeys as credentials synced between a person’s devices through a cloud service, and device-bound passkeys as ones that never leave a single device, such as those on a security key. Attestation. Evidence about the make and model of an authenticator, which a relying party can ask for at registration. Authenticator assurance levels (AAL). NIST SP 800-63B uses these to describe how much confidence a sign-in gives. In the current revision, applications assessed at AAL2 have to offer a phishing-resistant option, and AAL3 requires a non-exportable private key and phishing resistance. Authentication strength.

Microsoft Entra’s name for a conditional access control that requires a set of methods. It has three built-in strengths: multifactor, passwordless and phishing-resistant. Phishing-resistant includes FIDO2 security keys, Windows Hello for Business or a platform credential, and certificate-based authentication. I use Microsoft Entra as the worked example because its documentation is public and I checked it for this page. The same slots exist in other identity providers.

x: There are four parts on the normal path and two on the side.
