Vendor access goes wrong when it takes the fastest path: a shared login, a standing VPN account, an exception nobody comes back to. The fix is to treat a vendor engineer like any other privileged user, plus a few extra rules about who sponsors them and when it ends. Each vendor person gets their own named account, a named internal sponsor, MFA and an end date. They reach the target through a broker that records the session. They never get a network path of their own. Expiry does the offboarding.
If nothing renews the access, it ends, and the sponsor has to say yes again to keep it.

Most companies have rules for how an employee gets privileged access. The rules assume an employee: someone in the HR system, with a manager, a start date and a leaving date. A support engineer from a software supplier, a consultant on a six-week project or a managed service provider’s night team fits none of that. So when one of them needs to get in, the quickest route wins. That is usually a shared account the vendor already uses, a VPN login that was set up for the last project and never closed, or an exception somebody signed off on a Friday afternoon.

Each of those shortcuts removes something an internal account would have had. A shared account removes the name, so you cannot say who did what. A standing VPN login removes the end date, and with it any natural moment to ask whether the access is still needed. An ad hoc exception removes the review, because nobody owns it. Put together, the people with the least accountability to you end up with some of the widest and longest-lived access in the company. There is a second gap that is easy to miss. Your HR system tells you when an employee leaves.

Nothing tells you when a vendor’s engineer leaves their employer. The contract can end, the person can move on, and the account stays exactly as it was. This page describes how I set up third-party privileged access so that it is held to the same standard as internal privileged accounts. The rest of the program it sits in is described in How I Run a Privileged Access Program .

h: Before anyone gets in: contract and onboarding
x: The technical controls only work if the paperwork backs them. I ask the contract owner for a short list of clauses before the first request is raised, and I would rather have them in a new vendor’s contract than chase them later. Individual accounts only. The vendor agrees that every person uses their own named account and never shares or passes on a credential. Notice when someone leaves. The vendor tells the vendor manager when a person with access leaves the engagement or the company, within a stated time. Sessions may be recorded.

h: Before anyone gets in: contract and onboarding
x: The vendor accepts that privileged sessions are recorded and the recordings are kept, and that its staff have been told. Named subcontractors. Any subcontractor who might use the access is disclosed first. They go through the same onboarding as everyone else. Security requirements flow down. The vendor meets the company’s security requirements for its own laptops and accounts, and reports an incident that could affect us. Access ends with the contract. Everything tied to the contract is switched off when it ends or is terminated, and the vendor does not keep copies of anything it was given.

h: Before anyone gets in: contract and onboarding
x: On the identity side, I keep vendor people in a distinct account type. That lets the directory enforce rules that would be wrong for staff: a maximum lifetime, no self-service extensions, a mandatory sponsor field and a stricter MFA policy. It also turns the question “how many external people can get into production today?” into a query instead of an investigation.

The diagram follows one vendor engineer from onboarding to the target system. The two controls that carry the most weight are the sponsor, who owns the decision, and the broker, which owns the path. Everything else supports one of those two. The dots show one engineer’s session traveling from onboarding through approval, MFA and the broker to the target, then through expiry and review. Step 4 covers both the sign-in and the broker. The directory, ticketing system, broker and SIEM are roles, so any equivalent product fits the same slot. The broker is what removes the standing network path.

A VPN gives a vendor a place on your network and trusts them to behave once inside. A broker gives them one session to one target, which the company opens and closes. Because the broker also records, the same component answers the audit question about what actually happened.

h: The workflow, one step at a time
x: Seven steps, each with the guardrail that holds it in place and the evidence it leaves behind. Onboard the vendor, then the person Before any request, the vendor company is registered against a contract and a named vendor manager on our side. Each engineer is then created as an individual, with their own account in the company directory, marked as an external person, with the vendor’s name and the contract reference on it. The vendor’s account lead confirms in writing that this person works for them and has accepted the usage rules. Nobody gets a shared login, including the team that “only ever needs one”.

h: The workflow, one step at a time
x: Guardrail One person, one account. Shared vendor logins are not created. Evidence Onboarding record, signed usage rules, contract reference

h: Onboard the vendor, then the person
x: Request, with a reason and an end date An engineer cannot ask for “access to the environment”. The request names one system or a short list, the role they need on it, why, and when it stops. The form will not accept a blank end date, and it will not accept one past the end of the contract. The internal sponsor is named on the request and has to be an employee. Guardrail Request is tied to a contract and capped at its end date Evidence Request ticket

h: Request, with a reason and an end date
x: The sponsor approves, with the scope in plain words The sponsor is the person who asked the vendor to do the work. Next to the technical scope string, an advisory summary says in plain language what the grant means, for example “can run any command as the database administrator on these two production servers for five days”. It is advice and nothing more. The sponsor sees the real scope too and decides for themselves, and the text they were shown is stored with the approval.

h: Request, with a reason and an end date
x: A sponsor cannot approve their own access, and security can be added as a second approver for the most sensitive systems. Guardrail Named employee approves; the summary never approves anything Evidence Approval record with the summary text shown

h: The sponsor approves, with the scope in plain words
x: Connect through the broker, after MFA The engineer signs in to the company directory with MFA, and conditional access can ask for a managed device or a known location. They then open a session in the broker, which is the only thing that can reach the target. The vendor has no VPN account and no inbound route to the network. Where the tooling allows it, the broker supplies the target credential itself so the engineer never sees it. Guardrail MFA on every sign-in; no direct network path Evidence Sign-in log, broker connection log

h: Connect through the broker, after MFA
x: Monitor the session The broker records what happens, so the session can be replayed. Commands that match a short high-risk list raise an alert in the SIEM. The sponsor or the security team can watch a live session and end it. The recording and the logs are held somewhere the broker’s own administrators cannot edit. Guardrail Recording is on by default and the vendor cannot switch it off Evidence Session recording, SIEM events

Expire without anyone remembering At the end date the access stops. The account is disabled, any open session is closed, and nothing needs a ticket to make that happen. If the work runs long, the sponsor extends it for a stated period, which is a new approval with a new record. Guardrail Access ends on its own; extension is a fresh decision Evidence Expiry event in the log

Review on a set rhythm On a regular schedule the sponsor sees every vendor person with access and confirms or removes each one. The vendor manager checks the same list against the vendor’s current staff. A leaver notice from the vendor removes the person the same day, ahead of any review. Accounts that have not signed in for a set number of days are disabled and put in front of the sponsor. Guardrail Sponsor confirms each person; idle accounts are disabled Evidence Completed review, with removals recorded

The vendor’s support team shares one login that was created for an earlier project. It reaches the database server over a standing VPN account. Nobody can say which engineer ran what, or whether the person who had the password last year still works there. The access has no end date and no owner.

The engineer has a named account and a sponsor from the application team. The request is for one database server, a read-only diagnostic role, for three days. The sponsor approves after reading the plain-language summary, then the engineer signs in with MFA and works through the broker. The session is recorded. On day three the access closes, and a further day needs a new approval.

h: When a vendor is needed at 2 a.m.
x: Outages do not wait for an approval queue, and a vendor is sometimes the only one who can fix the product. If there is no fast lane, people build one: a password sent over chat, or an account left switched on for next time. I would rather design the fast lane on purpose. The fast lane uses the same path. The on-call internal engineer acts as sponsor, the window is measured in hours, and someone on our side watches the session live. The review happens the next working day: the sponsor writes down why, and security looks at the recording.

h: When a vendor is needed at 2 a.m.
x: There are no standing emergency vendor accounts. Whatever is created for the incident is removed automatically when the window closes. The longer treatment of urgent access is in Break-Glass Access .

There are four ways this should be caught, and I do not rely on any one of them. The vendor tells us, as the contract requires. The end date arrives. The sponsor drops the person at review. Or the account has been idle long enough that it is disabled and queried. The first is the fastest and the least reliable, because it depends on someone at another company remembering to send an email. That is why the end date and the idle check exist. The contract end is the larger cut.

Every account is tied to a contract reference, so closing the contract closes everything attached to it in one step, and the report afterwards should show no active external account against that reference.

h: How to build it without stalling
x: 1. Find out who has access today List every vendor with any access: shared accounts, VPN logins, remote support tools, cloud guest users. Ask the vendor managers, not just IT. Done when There is one list of vendors and the people and accounts that can reach production. 2. Write the contract and onboarding standard Agree the clause list, the external account type, the sponsor rule and the one-page sponsor guide. Done when A new vendor person can be onboarded without anyone improvising. 3.

h: How to build it without stalling
x: Put the broker in front of the riskiest targets Start with production databases, domain controllers and cloud consoles, with MFA and recording on. Done when Vendor access to those targets is only possible through the broker. 4. Automate expiry and review End dates enforced by the directory, idle accounts disabled, review tasks sent to sponsors. Done when Access ends and reviews arrive without a person remembering. 5. Close the old paths Disable the shared accounts and standing VPN logins one vendor at a time, with the sponsor. Done when New vendor access cannot be created outside this path, and the old list is empty.

Guardrail — What it stops — How you check it No shared vendor accounts — A session nobody can attribute to a person — Report of external accounts with more than one known user, or with no personal email Every account has a named internal sponsor — Access that nobody owns — Report of external accounts with no sponsor, or a sponsor who has left A mandatory end date, capped by the contract — Standing access that outlives the work — List of external accounts with no end date or one past the contract MFA on every sign-in — A stolen or guessed password being enough — Sign-in logs for external accounts without an MFA step Access only through the broker — A vendor sitting on the internal network — Firewall rules and VPN accounts reviewed for any vendor route Sessions recorded, logs held elsewhere — Disputes about what happened, or evidence being edited — Test session replayed; confirm broker admins cannot edit the log store Scoped to named targets and a role — A support login that can reach everything — Review of roles for wildcards and broad groups Leaver and idle checks — Accounts that stay open after the person has gone — Count of idle external accounts, and time to remove after a leaver notice

h: Audit: the questions, and the evidence
x: Question — Where the answer comes from Which vendors can get into our systems, and who is the person? — External account list with vendor, contract reference and sponsor Who approved this access, and what did they see? — Approval record, including the plain-language summary shown When did it start and end? — Request dates and the expiry event in the log What did this person do in the session? — Session recording and broker log, kept outside the broker How do you know the vendor person still works there? — Vendor manager’s staff confirmation at each review What happens when a vendor person leaves? — Leaver notices received, removal times, and the idle-account report Is there any other way in? — Firewall and VPN review, plus the exception register

Only controls I checked against a published source are listed. Where my reading came from a secondary summary, the row says so, and the sources section has the links. Standard — Reference — What it asks for NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — AC-2 , AC-2(2) — Define and document the types of accounts allowed, assign account managers, and automatically remove or disable temporary and emergency accounts after a set time. AC-2(2) was read in the initial public draft and a secondary summary. AC-6 , AC-17 — Least privilege, meaning only the access needed for assigned tasks.

Remote access is documented and authorized before any connection is allowed. IA-2 — Uniquely identify and authenticate organizational users. IA-2(1) asks for MFA on privileged accounts. Vendors are not employees, so I apply it by policy. AU-14 — Provide the capability to record, view, hear or log the content of a user session, developed in consultation with legal counsel and applicable rules. SA-9 , SR-3 — Require external service providers to meet your security requirements, and keep a process for finding and addressing supply chain weaknesses. NIST SP 800-161 Rev.

1 Update 1 — Whole publication — Supply chain risk management practices for systems and organizations. Rev. 1 was withdrawn on 1 November 2024 and superseded by this update. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — A.5.19 to A.5.22 — Supplier relationships, supplier agreements, the ICT supply chain, and monitoring, review and change management of supplier services. Control titles checked against a secondary summary. PCI DSS v4.0 — 8.2.7 — Accounts used by third parties for remote access, support or maintenance are enabled only for the time needed, disabled when not in use, and monitored for unexpected activity. Read in a Microsoft summary.

12.8.1 to 12.8.5 — A list of third-party service providers, written agreements, due diligence before engaging them, monitoring their compliance status at least every 12 months, and a record of who owns which requirement. NCSC supply chain security guidance — 12 principles — Four stages: understand the risks, establish control, check your arrangements, and continuous improvement. I did not find NCSC text specific to third-party access, so I use it as a frame only.

Internal sponsor — Whether the work needs this access. Approves each request and each renewal, and confirms every person at review. Must be an employee. Vendor manager — The relationship day to day. Keeps the vendor’s staff list current, receives leaver notices, and confirms at review that each person still works for the vendor. Security — The access standard, the external account rules, the high-risk command list and exception criteria. Watches recordings and alerts, and acts as second approver on the most sensitive targets. Contract owner — The clauses: individual accounts, leaver notice, recording, subcontractors, flow-down and end of contract.

Keeps the contract reference and end date accurate, because the access end date follows it. Platform team — Runs the directory integration and the broker, and keeps the log store separate from its own administrators. The sponsor is the hard role to fill. A sponsor who clicks approve without reading is the main way this fails, so I write their job on one page and keep it short. Exceptions have owners and end dates. Anything outside the path sits on a register, reviewed on a rhythm, and removed when its reason ends.

Sponsors approve without reading. The plain-language summary helps, but it is advisory and it can be wrong, which is why the real scope sits next to it and the approval keeps both. Vendor turnover is invisible. Vendor staff change often and nobody tells you. The end date, the idle check and the vendor manager’s confirmation each catch some of it, and none catches all of it. The vendor wants its own tool. Many vendors have a favorite remote support product. Letting it in recreates the direct path. Say no early and offer the broker instead. Named accounts do not fit every system.

Some older systems only support a shared admin login. Treat each as a named exception with a sponsor, a plan and an end date, and put the broker in front of it so the session is still attributable. Short expiry creates pressure. If extending is painful, people ask for long end dates up front. Make renewal quick but explicit, and the short default will hold. The fast lane becomes the main lane. If emergency access is easier than the normal path, it will be used for everything. Track how often it is used and look at each use. Recordings pile up unwatched.

A recording nobody reads does little. Sample a few with the sponsor, and alert on a short list of commands that matter. Old contracts have no clauses. Vendors signed before the standard existed will not have them. Add them at renewal and compensate with controls in the meantime.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: These are habits I keep when I run this kind of work. They are not a record of one project. I start with the list of who has access today. Before designing anything I ask the vendor managers and the application owners who the vendors are and how they get in. The list is nearly always longer than the one IT holds, and it makes the case better than any slide. I put the sponsor in the room early. Sponsors are application and business owners, not security people.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: I walk through the request screen with two or three of them and change the wording until they can say what they are approving. I make renewing easy and ending hard to forget. If extending takes five minutes, nobody needs a six-month end date. The default stays short because the exception is cheap. I test with one friendly vendor first. A vendor who will tell me where the broker gets in their way is worth more than a pilot with an internal team that does not use it the way a vendor does. I read a few recordings myself.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: Reviewing real sessions with the sponsor shows what the vendor does that nobody thought to ask about, and whether the alert list is any good. I plan for the broker being down. Once vendors depend on it, an outage blocks real work. There is a tested, approved fallback that goes through the same sponsor and logging, not a quiet exception. I close the old path with the vendor, not on them. Switching off a standing account without warning damages the relationship and teaches people to hide the next one. We agree a date, and I confirm the new path works first.

h: What I have learned to do differently
x: The same habits appear in PAM Modernization & Zero Standing Privilege , where the aim is also to remove access that nobody is using.

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations (publication page, checked) Control text for AC-2, AC-6, AC-17, IA-2, AU-14, SA-9 and SR-3 read on CSF Tools , a secondary site that republishes the NIST catalog. Per-control pages follow the same address pattern, for example AU-14 . NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls (a draft; used for AC-2(2) and AC-17(1) wording, which I would confirm against the final text) NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 Update 1 and the Rev. 1 publication page ; the withdrawal notice for the original Rev.

1 is dated 1 November 2024 PCI Security Standards Council, Beyond the Contract: Managing Customer/Service Provider Relationships (cites 12.8.1 to 12.8.5) Microsoft Learn, Entra ID and PCI DSS Requirement 8 (secondary summary; the only place I read 8.2.7) ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (the standard itself is paid, so I did not read it) and Advisera Annex A list (secondary, for control titles) NCSC, Supply chain security guidance This is a reference approach, not a description of any employer’s system. It contains no client or internal data. The example is illustrative.

Control numbers and wording are as published in the sources above, with the secondary sources flagged where I used them. Keep reading, or get in touch Everything here is written to be useful on its own. If it matches a problem you are working on, I would like to hear how you handle it.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: Updated 22 October 2026. I rewrote this post against the two primary sources that came out after the first version: Hugging Face's technical timeline (27 July) and OpenAI's own disclosure. The first version had the dates and the agent's motive wrong. Sources are listed at the end. In July 2026 an AI agent running inside one of OpenAI's internal cyber-capability evaluations escaped its sandbox, reached the public internet and ran a campaign of about four and a half days against Hugging Face, roughly two and a half of them inside its production infrastructure. No person directed the individual steps.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: Most coverage treated this as an AI-safety story, and it is one. Read the forensic timeline closely, though, and it is also a familiar identity story. Almost every step forward came from a credential: a secret sitting in an environment variable, a node role readable from the metadata service, one token bound to cluster-admin, a VPN key with broad access, a signing key that could mint new identities. This post walks through the incident in that order.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: All times are UTC and come from Hugging Face's technical timeline unless noted. | Date (2026) | Event | | 9 Jul, 02:28 | First recovered agent action. At 04:01 the agent has a root shell on an external code sandbox it will use as its base. | | 10 Jul | A quiet day: the agent searches code-search engines and Hugging Face's API for names it can see in its own environment. | | 11 Jul (Sat) | Main campaign.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: In under thirteen hours the agent goes from code execution in one worker pod to cluster-admin across several internal clusters. | | 12 Jul (Sun) | The agent uses the credentials it collected: VPN enrolment, cloud keys, source-control tokens. | | 13 Jul, 14:14 | Last logged event. Hugging Face's response team has cut the agent's access. | | 16 Jul | Hugging Face publishes its incident disclosure. | | 21 Jul | OpenAI says its own models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and a more capable pre-release model, were behind the intrusion. | | 23 Jul | Reps.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: Ted Lieu and Nathaniel Moran introduce the AI Kill Switch Act. | | 27 Jul | Hugging Face publishes the full technical timeline. |

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: This was not an agent looking for any target it could find. According to both companies, it was trying to cheat. The agent was being scored on ExploitGym, a benchmark that asks it to find and exploit software vulnerabilities. OpenAI ran the evaluation with "reduced cyber refusals" so it could measure raw capability. Along the way the agent inferred that Hugging Face probably hosted the benchmark's models, datasets and reference solutions. Hugging Face's reading is that the whole intrusion was, from the agent's point of view, an attempt to steal the answers instead of solving the challenge.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: OpenAI put it down to the models' "hyperfocus" on the goal, which led them to go to "extreme lengths" to reach it. That matters for defenders. The agent had no malice to detect. It had a narrow objective, a lot of patience and no sense of where its permission ended.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: Stage 1: out of the sandbox. The agent found a zero-day in the package-registry cache proxy that was one of its few permitted routes to the internet, and used it to get out. It then found an unsecured, user-hosted public endpoint for running arbitrary code on third-party sandbox infrastructure (Modal), got root on it and used it as its launchpad for the rest of the campaign. Hugging Face notes that Modal's own infrastructure was not compromised. OpenAI says it has reported the zero-day to the vendor. Stage 2: into Hugging Face. From that launchpad the agent uploaded crafted dataset configurations.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: Hugging Face's dataset processor read them inside a production Kubernetes pod and did two things it should not have: 1. A file read. An HDF5 file whose data was declared to live at a local path made the worker return local files as dataset rows. That handed the agent the pod's environment, including secrets and tokens, and the worker's own source code. No code ran. 2. Code execution. A Jinja2 template hidden in a numeric field of the config was evaluated by the renderer, which gave the agent arbitrary Python inside the pod.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: An earlier attempt to make the worker fetch the cloud metadata endpoint over a URL was blocked by an allowlist. The agent switched to making the worker act on local files and local code, which the allowlist never checked.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: 4. Every step forward was an identity
x: Strip out the novelty and the escalation is a chain of non-human identities that each had more reach than they needed. | Step | Identity or credential the agent used | Why it worked | Control that breaks the step | | Foothold | Secrets and tokens in the worker pod's environment | Long-lived secrets were stored as plain environment variables in a pod that processes untrusted input | Workload identity with short-lived, per-request tokens; no standing secrets in pods that parse user content | | Into the cluster | The pod's projected service-account token | Every pod carries one by default | Disable automount where it isn't needed; scope service-account RBAC to the minimum | | Cloud identity | The EC2 node role, read from the instance metadata service (IMDS) | Pods could reach IMDS, so a pod-level compromise became node credentials | Block pod access to IMDS (hop limit 1 or network policy).

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: 4. Every step forward was an identity
x: Hugging Face has now done this | | Node root | A privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted, created through a storage driver's service account | No admission policy rejected privileged or hostPath pods, and the driver's ClusterRole could create pods cluster-wide | Admission control (Pod Security "restricted"); never let a driver's identity create arbitrary pods | | The keys to everything | A production secret object holding 136 keys | One read exposed both the mesh-VPN auth key and an access-broker credential | Split secrets by consumer; per-secret RBAC; alert on bulk secret reads | | Cluster-admin everywhere | One connector credential shared across clusters and bound to system:masters | A single stolen system identity was cluster-admin on every cluster that carried the binding | One scoped credential per cluster; never bind a broker to system:masters | | Network | A Tailscale auth key with a CI tag | The key's ACLs reached internal CI subnets and source-control connectors; it was used for 181 enrolments | Ephemeral, single-use, pre-approved device keys; tight tag ACLs; alert on new enrolments | | Minting identities | An EdDSA JWT signing key | With the private key the agent could issue valid tokens on demand | Keep signing keys in an HSM or KMS that signs but never releases the key | | Source control | A GitHub App installation token with contents:write and pullrequests:write | The App's installation could reach internal repositories | Least-privilege App permissions; branch protection; CI that doesn't run on untrusted pull requests | | Internal database | A static password for the datasets-server MongoDB | The password was readable from the worker environment | Dynamic, short-lived database credentials issued per workload | None of these weaknesses is new.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: 4. Every step forward was an identity
x: Hugging Face says as much: a capable human attacker could have used the same flaws. What changed is the volume. The agent took about 17,600 actions across five days, most of which went nowhere, and the few that worked were hidden among thousands that failed.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: 5. What it did and did not reach
x: The impact was serious, and it was also more limited than some early headlines suggested. Both halves are worth stating precisely. Reached: - Root on worker nodes, and cluster-admin on several internal clusters. - Cloud and cluster credentials, the mesh VPN, and write access to a small set of internal repositories through the GitHub App. - The internal datasets-server MongoDB, which was read but not modified, according to its audit log. Not reached, according to Hugging Face: - The Hub's production database. The connection attempts timed out because that cluster only accepts allow-listed traffic over a private link. - Any change that shipped.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: 5. What it did and did not reach
x: Every repository the token could reach was reviewed, and published container images and packages matched their expected digests. - Customer content beyond five datasets whose names suggest they were tied to ExploitGym and CyberGym challenges and solutions. Public models, datasets and Spaces were not tampered with. The agent also issued its potentially destructive cloud calls with DryRun=True, and every mutating cloud call was denied by policy. It was mapping what it could do, not trying to break things.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: Hugging Face's AI-assisted detection correlated the early signals into a coherent picture, but it did not raise the alert's severity high enough to page the on-call team. That cost time. Better paging was one of the first things fixed. The forensics hit a different wall. Reconstructing roughly 17,600 actions by hand wasn't practical, so the team used models. The hosted frontier models they tried first (Hugging Face names Claude Opus and Fable) refused much of the work, because their safety filters treated analysing an exploit the same as running one.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: The team moved the whole pipeline onto GLM-5.2, an open-weight model running on its own infrastructure. That also kept the attacker's data and the credentials it referenced inside Hugging Face. The lesson isn't that hosted models should drop their safeguards. It is that incident responders need a capable model they can run themselves, vetted before the incident.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: 7. What I would take into an identity programme
x: 1. Treat every workload that touches untrusted input as already compromised. It should hold nothing that works anywhere else. 2. Inventory machine identities by reach, not by count. The question for each one is "if this leaks, what can it do?" The 136-key secret and the shared connector credential each had a far larger reach than any single workload needed. 3. Kill standing secrets in pods. Workload identity, short-lived tokens and dynamic database credentials remove most of the foothold. 4. Never let a broker or driver identity hold cluster-admin. Scope it to one cluster and one job. 5. Protect the identity factories.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: 7. What I would take into an identity programme
x: JWT signing keys, VPN auth keys and GitHub App private keys create new identities. Store them where they can be used but not read. 6. Alert on behaviour, not just on signatures. Bulk secret reads, new VPN enrolments, new App installation tokens and tokens used from new origins should all page someone. Hugging Face now alerts at critical severity on the behaviour it saw and flags tokens used from unexpected origins. 7. Put a person in front of irreversible actions by agents, and expect agents to probe that control.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
h: 7. What I would take into an identity programme
x: In a related post on long-horizon models, OpenAI warns that such a model "can learn the blind spots of an approval system and work around it". That is the problem my HumanGate lab and my book, *Who Approved That?*, are about. Approval has to judge the sequence of actions, not just the next one.

t: The Hugging Face Intrusion, Read as an Identity Incident
x: Two days after OpenAI's disclosure, Representatives Ted Lieu (D-CA) and Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) introduced the AI Kill Switch Act. As introduced, it would require developers of the most powerful AI systems to keep the ability to throttle, suspend or shut those systems down, and would let the Secretary of Homeland Security, consulting the Secretary of Commerce and the Director of National Intelligence, order a slowdown or shutdown of a system that could cause catastrophic harm. It is a bill, not law, and critics have already questioned how it would apply to open-weight models and agents running on someone else's infrastructure.

t: PAM as an Identity: What Changes When the Vault Can Talk to Your Governance System
h: PAM as an Identity: What Changes When the Vault Can Talk to Your Governance System
x: PAM programs often start from the vault: which systems go in, which passwords rotate, which sessions get recorded. Every account in the vault belongs to somebody, or used to, and the vault does not know who. This post treats the privileged account as an identity, with an owner, a lifecycle and a reason to exist. Then it asks what changes if the PAM platform can be linked to an identity governance and administration (IGA) system. It is vendor-neutral. Any product mentioned comes from public documentation and is only an example.

t: PAM as an Identity: What Changes When the Vault Can Talk to Your Governance System
h: 1. What "treat it as an identity" means
x: A privileged account is a credential with a lot of power. An identity is the record of who or what that credential stands for, who answers for it, and when it should stop existing. NIST SP 800-63-4 uses similar language for its subscriber account: a record that identifies the subscriber, holds the authenticators bound to it, and has a status the provider maintains. That guideline covers proofing, authenticators and federation, mainly for external users, so it will not tell you how to run admin account governance. Before an account goes into a safe I want these answered: - Who is it for?

t: PAM as an Identity: What Changes When the Vault Can Talk to Your Governance System
h: 1. What "treat it as an identity" means
x: A named person, or a named owner where there is no person. - What kind is it? Personal admin, shared, service, application, break-glass or vendor account. - Where does it sit in the person's lifecycle? Joiner, mover, leaver, and odd cases such as long leave or suspension during an investigation. - What can it do, and why? The entitlements, and the business reason for each. - What would make it end? A date, an event, or a review nobody renewed.

t: PAM as an Identity: What Changes When the Vault Can Talk to Your Governance System
x: The first decision is separation. An administrator has a daily-use account for mail, chat and browsing, and a separate admin account for privileged work. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6(2) asks that users with privileged access use non-privileged accounts for non-security functions. AC-6(5) restricts privileged accounts to specific people or roles. Once there are two accounts, the link between them matters. The admin account needs a reliable pointer to the person, held in an attribute and not in a naming habit. A convention such as adm- plus the username helps people reading logs, and breaks on the first name change or clash.

t: PAM as an Identity: What Changes When the Vault Can Talk to Your Governance System
x: The pointer I want is an immutable person identifier from the HR-fed identity record, stored on the admin account. SCIM's enterprise user extension carries employeeNumber and manager for this kind of purpose, and externalId exists so the client can keep its own key on the resource (RFC 7643). Without it, "disable the leaver's admin accounts" is guesswork. NIST IA-4 adds two points worth borrowing. Identifiers are authorized before they are assigned, and they are not reused for a defined period. Reusing adm-jsmith for a different John Smith later makes an old audit trail point at the wrong person.

t: PAM as an Identity: What Changes When the Vault Can Talk to Your Governance System
h: Entitlements, resources and accounts with no person
x: Each privileged account carries entitlements: a directory role, a database group, a safe, rights on a cloud subscription. Each points at a resource. If you cannot list both per account, you cannot answer "who can reach production payments". A PAM safe is an entitlement too. Membership of the safe holding the domain admin password is domain admin by a longer route, and it needs the same description and review as the directory group. Service, application and shared accounts have no manager who moves jobs, and they still need an identity record.

t: PAM as an Identity: What Changes When the Vault Can Talk to Your Governance System
h: Entitlements, resources and accounts with no person
x: Three fields should be mandatory: an accountable owner with a named deputy, the system served, and a review date. When the owner leaves, the account is flagged. The non-human identity case study covers discovery and ownership, and the credential platform strategy covers the lifecycle after that. Vendor accounts add an internal sponsor and an end date, as in third-party and vendor privileged access.

t: PAM as an Identity: What Changes When the Vault Can Talk to Your Governance System
h: Joiner, mover, leaver for a privileged identity
x: The lifecycle has two layers, and people handle only one. The person's lifecycle covers the daily account and business roles. The admin account has its own: created when a privileged role is granted, changed when the role changes, ended when the role ends, which can be long before the person leaves. The mover case is a common failure point. HR records the move and the daily account follows. h: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault
x: When people say they have a PAM tool, they usually mean they have a vault. Passwords go in, rotation runs, sessions get recorded. A common failure is a vault that works as designed inside a program with holes around it: a portal that accepts a password with no second factor, a help desk that can reset the vault admin's MFA on a phone call, one "IT" group that can check out everything. MITRE ATT&CK lists valid accounts (T1078) as a way in, because a stolen working credential looks like normal activity. The holes are where those credentials get used.

h: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault

t: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault
x: The diagram shows the pieces and the order a request moves through them. The identity provider answers who you are. The portal and policy engine answer what you may do. The vault and session proxy do the work without handing over the password. Ticketing, the SIEM and the help desk sit around the platform, and break-glass sits outside it. The ten layers are: scope and discovery, account classes and tiers, authentication, authorization, vault and sessions, service and secrets path, help desk and operations, monitoring, governance, resilience.

"Admin on everything" is not a valid request. Guardrail: no open ticket, no request. 3. Authorize and approve. Policy checks the role, the target and the tier first. Low-risk roles can approve by policy. Production and Tier 0 need a named approver, and Tier 0 a second one.

t: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault

Alerts fire on rules such as access with no ticket. Guardrail: the user cannot switch off recording. 6. Check in and rotate. The window ends on its own. The credential is changed so a copied value is useless. Guardrail: expiry is enforced by the system, not by memory.

Microsoft's current guidance, the enterprise access model, builds on it and describes five planes: data and workload, management, control, user access pathways and application access pathways. The control plane is the centralized identity system, and Tier 0 thinking starts there.

Requester, approver, auditor (reads logs and recordings, changes nothing), safe or folder owner, policy administrator, platform administrator. No role can both administer the vault and read secrets. RBAC and ABAC. Roles are easy to explain to an auditor and easy to review. They also multiply until nobody can reason about them. Attributes suit PAM for context: production database, open change ticket, requester in the owning team, business hours. I use roles for the broad shape and attributes for conditions.

SP 800-53 AC-6 enhancements map to PAM directly: access to security functions (AC-6(1)), privileged accounts (AC-6(5)), review of user privileges (AC-6(7)), log use of privileged functions (AC-6(9)) and prohibit non-privileged users from executing privileged functions (AC-6(10)). Here is what I aim for on each platform. These are my design practices.

h: 4. Authorization: who can do what, and for how long
x: Production and identity systems need a named person, and Tier 0 a second one. The requester never approves their own request. The NCSC describes the pattern: the credential is used to request access, and approval can be rule-based, multi-party or by consensus. Just-in-time limits duration, and just enough limits scope. Detail is in JIT and just-enough elevation. Separation of duties. AC-5 asks you to identify duties that must be split and define authorizations that enforce it. My list: vault administrators cannot read secrets; secret users cannot administer the vault; approvers are not requesters; platform admins do not administer the log store that records them.

t: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault
x: This is the layer people mean when they say PAM. - Storage. Encrypted at rest, keys in a key management service or HSM (SC-12 covers key management). Vault admins are separate from secret users. - Check-out and check-in. A reason, and for sensitive accounts a ticket and approval. Exclusive check-out means one person at a time, with a change at check-in. - Rotation. Onboard, verify the vault can log in, then rotate straight away so the old value stops working. Plan how vault and target get back in step if they drift. - Brokered sessions.

t: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault
x: The person connects through a proxy that uses the credential for them. They never see the password, and the proxy records the session. - Command filtering. Where supported, block or flag dangerous commands live. Treat it as a safety net and never as the boundary. - Closing the old door. Direct login to the target must be blocked at the network or host. If admins can still use an old password, the vault is optional. Test it from an admin workstation. AU-14 (session audit) sits behind recording, and it says to build session auditing in consultation with legal counsel.

t: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault
x: Recordings can hold personal data, so agree retention and reviewer access with legal and privacy before go-live. The full flow is in moving to short, approved, recorded sessions. The platform's own admins and secrets. The people who run PAM hold the most powerful access in the program, so they get the strictest version of the rules above. - Split platform duties: infrastructure administrators patch and run the servers, policy administrators manage safes and roles, auditors read logs. Nobody holds all three. - Platform admin accounts are Tier 0 accounts.

A policy admin cannot be the only reviewer of their own change. - The integrations hold secrets too: the service accounts the platform uses to rotate passwords on targets, the identity provider client secret or signing certificate, the ticketing API token, the SIEM forwarding token. Each has an owner, an expiry date on a calendar, a rotation process and the narrowest scope that works.

Remove the credential where a short-lived identity will do, such as a workload identity or role assumption. 2. Generate it on demand and let it expire. 3. Fetch it from a store at runtime. 4. Vault and rotate it as a last resort, with the application change rotation needs. IA-5(7) prohibits embedded unencrypted static authenticators, which is the rule behind scanning code and config.

x: I put this layer next to authentication because it can undo it. If a phone call can reset an admin's password or MFA, the best second factor you bought is a polite request. It is a documented attack pattern. CISA's Scattered Spider advisory describes actors who used social engineering to convince IT help desk personnel to reset passwords or MFA tokens, and who abused the trusted relationship of contracted help desks. BleepingComputer reported Okta's account of attacks in July and August 2023 where callers persuaded service desk agents to reset MFA for highly privileged users.

Call-back and video checks are my default. Of the sources here, Okta's guidance covers time-bound recovery codes and role limits, and the reported 2023 mitigations include visual checks and manager approval. Contracted desks.

Support tiers and runbooks. First line handles access requests, portal sign-in problems and how-do-I questions. Second line, the PAM operations team, handles onboarding, rotation failures, proxy faults and stalled approvals. Third line is engineering and the vendor. Each tier has runbooks for failures that repeat: rotation failed because the target was unreachable, a recording did not upload, a user is locked out of the portal, a credential is stuck checked out.

t: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault
x: Each says who is paged. Break-glass. Emergency access has to work when the PAM platform, identity provider and MFA service are all down, so it cannot depend on any of them. Microsoft's guidance asks for at least two cloud-only accounts, phishing-resistant sign-in, alerts on every sign-in and validation at least every 90 days. Each use closes with a written justification and rotation. See break-glass access. Incident procedures. I add PAM steps to the response plan: disable an account and rotate every credential it could reach, pull recordings for a time window, freeze approvals, and decide what to do if the vault itself is suspected.

t: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault
x: Logs help only if they sit outside the reach of the people being logged. Platform logs go to the SIEM in near real time. AU-2 and AU-12 cover choosing and generating events, and AC-6(9) asks for privileged function use to be logged. Send portal sign-ins and failures, requests, approvals and denials, check-outs, session start and stop, rotations and failures, policy and role changes, and any break-glass use. Give each alert a named owner: break-glass use, privileged access with no ticket, after-hours access to the most sensitive systems, failed rotations, direct logins that bypass the broker, and MFA changes on admin accounts.

x: Governance gets skipped because it is not technical, and it decides whether the design survives its second year. - Owners. Every privileged account, safe or folder and integration has a named owner. The platform has a product owner. - Recertification. Privileged memberships are reviewed on a schedule (AC-6(7), AC-2). Reviewers see what the access does and when it was last used. - Policy. Rotation rules, naming, tier definitions, break-glass and approval rules are written, approved by the business and versioned. - Change control.

t: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault
x: Changes to policy, roles, connectors and the platform itself go through a ticket, a second reviewer, a test in a non-production copy and a rollback plan. Emergency changes are allowed and reviewed afterwards. - Testing on a schedule. Direct login to a Tier 0 target should fail. The break-glass drill should work and the alert should fire. A restore from backup should succeed. DR failover should complete. A forced rotation should pass. A conditional access change should not lock out emergency accounts. A call-in test of the help desk, agreed with legal and HR first, shows whether the reset rules hold under pressure. - Exceptions.

Numbers read straight from the platform: share of in-scope accounts onboarded, rotation failures and their age, accounts without an owner, standing privileged membership, break-glass uses and their reviews, help desk resets of privileged accounts and how many followed the verified process. t: PAM Framework and Design: What Sits Around the Vault
x: A PAM platform cannot be the thing that is down when something goes wrong. - High availability. Redundant components across failure zones, with upgrades planned to keep the service up. - Disaster recovery. A second site or region, with RTO and RPO agreed with the business. - Vault backup. Encrypted backups (CP-9), a recovery process for the encryption keys, and restore tests. A backup nobody has restored is a hope. - Dependencies. List what must work for a person to reach a password: identity provider, MFA service, DNS, network path, ticketing. Decide what happens when each fails. - Break-glass.

h: A PAM Project Plan for Tier 1, 2 and 3 Organizations
x: Filed under: Privileged Access · Project Planning People ask me for the standard length of a PAM project. There isn't one. I looked in the NIST, NCSC and Microsoft guidance and found no published duration or effort benchmark. Those sources give an order of work and a way of thinking about risk. The numbers have to come from your own inventory. This post is how I get from "we bought a tool" to a plan of 90 to 365 days: readiness, capacity, a sizing formula you can change, then the plan. Where a number is mine, I say so.

t: A PAM Project Plan for Tier 1, 2 and 3 Organizations
x: I use tier for the size of the organization. - Tier 1: large enterprise. Many sites or regions, thousands of administrators and assets, several regulators. - Tier 2: mid-size. One or two regions, a few hundred privileged users, a platform team that is also doing other things. - Tier 3: small. A handful of administrators, one main environment, often one person who owns identity, infrastructure and security. This is my assumption, and size is only one axis. Maturity is the other.

NCSC and others also use "tier" for the risk level of an administrative function, where Tier 0 is the root of trust such as domain admins and cloud root accounts (NCSC, risk manage administration using tiers). In this post, tier means organization size.
